newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FUND VIEW - SBC Warburg goes neutral on Asia.
newsitem.headline: FUND VIEW - SBC Warburg goes neutral on Asia.

text.p: Volatility in U.S. dollar and interest rates threatens to unsettle Asian markets in the coming months, and investors should adopt a neutral position to avoid some of the worst upsets, SBC Warburg said.
"Although the short-term risk remains high, the risk of being in Asian markets is less than the risk of being out completely," Asian investment strategist Eugene Chung said.
Asia is reasonably well-positioned to cope with upward pressure in both U.S. rates and the dollar, with a tight monetary policy throughout most of the region and huge foreign exchange reserves.
"Nonethless, the risk of a stronger dollar and higher Fed Funds to Asia...is a prolonged period of weak export earnings, domestic demand and corporate profits," Chung said.

The strong U.S. dollar will delay the recovery of Asian exports. Even more worrisome, some Asian nations -- most notably Korea, Thailand and the Philippines -- have built up substantial U.S.-dollar liabilities from a capital expenditure binge over the past few years.

"It is not difficult to envisage that corporate cash flows will remain strained," Chung said. "We are experiencing the reversal of a decade of easy U.S. monetary policy, when cheap currency led to a downward bias in real interest rates in many regional economies."
Countries with the most currency flexibility will be the winners in such an environment.
Taiwan and Korea allowed their currencies to depreciate last year, thanks largely to their semi-closed capital accounts.
Although Hong Kong's currency is pegged to the U.S. dollar, Hong Kong should escape much of the damage thanks to Chinese exports, which have been the strongest in the region.
The real problems lie in Southeast Asia, where currencies are most inflexible and deflationary forces are most evident.
Singapore enjoys the most flexibility. Its dollar has already depreciated slightly and further easing was possible, Chung said.
Thailand, with US$39 billion in foreign liabilities and a banking sector in turmoil, has the least flexibility, and the Philippines bears the closest relation to Thailand.
An unsuccessful assault on the Thai baht last week, spurred by the country's slowing economy, sent jitters through other Asian countries as speculators turned on some regional currencies.

Thailand's weak economy, with growth seen slowing to a 10-year-low of around five percent, sluggish exports, high interest rates and ailing finance and property sectors have made it attractive prey for speculative attacks, analysts said.
The baht, fixed daily by the central bank against a basket of currencies heavily weighted in the dollar, was the target of similar attacks in February and late last year.
Excessive easy money has spawned asset price inflation in the Philippines over the past two years along with a sharp accumulation of foreign liabilities.

Most of these liabilities -- estimated at US$12.6 billion by SBC Warburg, or 146 percent of gross international reserves -- are unhedged, imposing the same sort of constraints on the central bank as in Thailand.

Exchange rates are slightly more flexible in Malaysia and Indonesia, suggesting that these markets should perform better. But Chung cautioned that Malaysian banks are heavily exposed to property and any further weakness in exports will add pressure to the currency.
One note of comfort -- statistics show that US$1.5 billion came into Asia ex-Japan from U.S. mutual funds compared to US$4.4 billion in 1993.

"This means that although the likelihood of increased international flows in the context of a rising bond yield is low, the risk of a large-scale pull-out of commitments is also low because more foreign investors are not overweight Asia ex-Japan," he said.

Chung recommends underweight Philippines and Malaysia, overweight Taiwan and Indonesia, and neutral through the rest of the region. SBC Warburg is also shifting two percent from Hong Kong to China (0.5 percent) and Singapore (1.5 percent).
